hints: A vector line needs a point and a direction; first find the position vectors of both \(M\) and \(N\).
Since \(M\) is the midpoint of \(OA\), halve \(\overrightarrow{OA}\); since \(AN:NB=2:1\), move two-thirds of the way from \(A\) to \(B\) to locate \(N\).

Use \(\overrightarrow{MN}=\overrightarrow{ON}-\overrightarrow{OM}\) as a direction and write \(\mathbf r=\overrightarrow{OM}+\lambda\overrightarrow{MN}\), allowing any non-zero scalar multiple of the direction.
walkthrough:
State the position vectors of $A$ and $B$:
$$\overrightarrow{OA} = 6\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j} = \begin{pmatrix} 6 \\ 2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \overrightarrow{OB} = 2\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j} + 3\mathbf{k} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$$

Find the position vector of $M$, the midpoint of $OA$:
$$\overrightarrow{OM} = \dfrac{1}{2}\overrightarrow{OA} = \dfrac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 6 \\ 2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = 3\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j}$$

Find the position vector of $N$ on $AB$ such that $AN = 2NB$ (dividing $AB$ in the ratio $2:1$):
$$\overrightarrow{ON} = \overrightarrow{OA} + \dfrac{2}{3}\overrightarrow{AB} = \overrightarrow{OA} + \dfrac{2}{3}\left(\overrightarrow{OB} - \overrightarrow{OA}\right) = \dfrac{1}{3}\overrightarrow{OA} + \dfrac{2}{3}\overrightarrow{OB}$$
$$\overrightarrow{ON} = \dfrac{1}{3}\begin{pmatrix} 6 \\ 2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + \dfrac{2}{3}\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 + 4/3 \\ 2/3 + 4/3 \\ 0 + 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 10/3 \\ 2 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} = \dfrac{10}{3}\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j} + 2\mathbf{k}$$

Find a direction vector for the line through $M$ and $N$:
$$\overrightarrow{MN} = \overrightarrow{ON} - \overrightarrow{OM} = \begin{pmatrix} 10/3 - 3 \\ 2 - 1 \\ 2 - 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1/3 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} = \dfrac{1}{3}\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} + 2\mathbf{k}$$
(Any non-zero scalar multiple, such as $\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j} + 6\mathbf{k}$, is equally valid as a direction vector.)

Write a vector equation for the line through $M$ and $N$, using $M$ as the base point:
$$\mathbf{r} = 3\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} + \lambda\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} + 2\mathbf{k}\right) \quad \left(\text{or } \mathbf{r} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} + \lambda\begin{pmatrix} 1/3 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}\right)$$

ai_rubric.Finding Equations of Straight Lines: Concludes that the position vector of \(M\) is \(3\mathbf i+\mathbf j\); Derives \(\frac{10}{3}\mathbf i+2\mathbf j+2\mathbf k\); Concludes with \(\displaystyle\mathbf r=3\mathbf i+\mathbf j+\lambda\left(\frac13\mathbf i+\mathbf j+2\mathbf k\right)\), or equivalent.

hints: Represent the line \(OB\) by \(\mathbf r=\mu(2\mathbf i+2\mathbf j+3\mathbf k)\), since it passes through the origin.
Equate this vector component-by-component to the line through \(M\) and \(N\) found in part (a).
Solve the resulting parameter equations consistently, then substitute the parameter into either line to obtain the position vector of \(P\).
walkthrough:
State the vector equation of the line passing through the origin $O$ and point $B(2, 2, 3)$:
$$\mathbf{r} = \mu\overrightarrow{OB} = \mu(2\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j} + 3\mathbf{k}) = \begin{pmatrix} 2\mu \\ 2\mu \\ 3\mu \end{pmatrix}$$

Equate the coordinates of the line $MN$ and the line $OB$ at their intersection point $P$:
$$3 + \dfrac{1}{3}\lambda = 2\mu \quad \text{--- (Equation 1)}$$
$$1 + \lambda = 2\mu \quad \text{--- (Equation 2)}$$
$$2\lambda = 3\mu \quad \text{--- (Equation 3)}$$

Equate Equation 1 and Equation 2 since both equal $2\mu$:
$$3 + \dfrac{1}{3}\lambda = 1 + \lambda$$
$$3 - 1 = \lambda - \dfrac{1}{3}\lambda$$
$$2 = \dfrac{2}{3}\lambda \implies \lambda = 2 \times \dfrac{3}{2} = 3$$

Substitute $\mu = 2$ into the equation of line $OB$ (or $\lambda = 3$ into line $MN$) to find the position vector of $P$:
$$\overrightarrow{OP} = 2(2\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j} + 3\mathbf{k}) = 4\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j} + 6\mathbf{k}$$
$$\left(\text{Check: } \overrightarrow{OP} = (3\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j}) + 3\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} + 2\mathbf{k}\right) = 4\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j} + 6\mathbf{k}\right)$$

ai_rubric.Using Position Vectors: Identifies \(\mathbf r=\mu(2\mathbf i+2\mathbf j+3\mathbf k)\) as the equation for \(OB\); Derives \(\lambda=3\) or \(\mu=2\), and position vector \(4\mathbf i+4\mathbf j+6\mathbf k\) for \(P\); Concludes with \(\overrightarrow{OP}=4\mathbf i+4\mathbf j+6\mathbf k\).

hints: For angle \(OPM\), form two vectors with common initial point \(P\): \(\overrightarrow{PO}=\overrightarrow{OO}-\overrightarrow{OP}\) and \(\overrightarrow{PM}=\overrightarrow{OM}-\overrightarrow{OP}\).
Evaluate the inverse cosine in degree mode and check that the chosen vector directions give the interior angle at \(P\).
walkthrough:
Identify the vectors originating from vertex $P$ defining angle $OPM$, namely $\overrightarrow{PO}$ and $\overrightarrow{PM}$:
$$\overrightarrow{PO} = -\overrightarrow{OP} = -(4\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j} + 6\mathbf{k}) = \begin{pmatrix} -4 \\ -4 \\ -6 \end{pmatrix}$$
$$\overrightarrow{PM} = \overrightarrow{OM} - \overrightarrow{OP} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 - 4 \\ 1 - 4 \\ 0 - 6 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ -3 \\ -6 \end{pmatrix} = -\mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j} - 6\mathbf{k}$$

Apply the cosine definition of the angle between two vectors $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\overrightarrow{PO} \cdot \overrightarrow{PM}}{|\overrightarrow{PO}| \,|\overrightarrow{PM}|}$:
$$\cos(\angle OPM) = \dfrac{52}{\sqrt{68} \times \sqrt{46}} = \dfrac{52}{\sqrt{3128}} \approx 0.929758$$

Calculate the angle $\angle OPM$ in degrees:
$$\angle OPM = \cos^{-1}(0.929758) \approx 21.6029^\circ$$

ai_rubric.Using Scalar Products: Calculates by the process for evaluating the scalar product of direction vectors for \(OP\) and \(MP\), or equivalent. Applies the process for the moduli, divide the scalar product by the product of the moduli and evaluates the inverse cosine of the result. Derives \(21.6^\circ\).
